newsitem.title: PERU: Peru abruptly calls off talks in hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru abruptly calls off talks in hostage crisis.

text.p: The Peruvian government abruptly called off negotiations with Marxist guerrillas holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence on Monday.
Government negotiator Domingo Palermo blamed the rebels for stalling the talks by cancelling a meeting last week alleging police had dug a tunnel under the besieged house.
Palermo said he did not attend a tenth round of talks scheduled for Monday because "the conditions for restarting preliminary conversations are still not sufficiently defined".

His position was due to a "deep-seated concern that the use of pretexts to unilaterally suspend conversations could be an attempt to reverse the valuable advances achieved so far," he said at a news conference.

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels cancelled talks planned for last Friday, accusing security forces of digging a tunnel to storm the diplomatic compound while rebel leaders were absent at the negotiations.
While the government has denied the existence of a tunnel, security force sources confirmed tunnels had been built.
Peruvians, nevertheless, widely believe the MRTA made the allegations to temporarily derail the talks and gain time.
After assurances from President Alberto Fujimori that he wanted to end the 11-week-old crisis peacefully, the rebels agreed on Sunday to return to the negotiating table.
Monday's abrupt suspension of the talks dashed renewed hopes for a bloodless outcome for the hostage drama.

Guarantors overseeing the talks also appeared surprised. The three-man commission and the Japanese government observer Terusuke Terada had arrived at a safe house across the street from the residence to attend the talks.
Until last week, the negotiations appeared to be advancing well with concrete proposals from both sides to end the siege.

Fujimori travelled to Cuba and got a promise from President Fidel Castro that the 20-odd rebels could receive asylum in Havana if all sides agreed. The offer of asylum in a foreign country appears to be one of the government's main bargaining chips in persuading the rebels to free their hostages.

"We hope both sides will meet as soon as possible given the situation of the hostages inside the residence," said Peru's Roman Catholic Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, one of the guarantors. "We will continue to make every effort to bring about a prompt and peaceful solution to this problem."
The rebels, however, said the siege would drag on due to the government's refusal to consider their main demand for the release of some 400 imprisoned comrades.

"There is no glimpse of a solution to the conflict because of the government's intransigence," read a communique sent to Reuters via e-mail from the MRTA's office in Hamburg. "The MRTA has made known its decision to contribute to a political solution to this crisis but at the same time we reaffirm the that this solution involves the freeing of our comrades."

The rebels seized more than 500 hostages when they stormed the residence on Dec. 17 during a diplomatic reception but have freed most of them. The remaining 72 captives in the mined and booby-trapped residence include two Peruvian ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and Fujimori's brother Pedro.
